name: Lauren Mitchell, Telemetry: adrenal crisis (Addison disease) after viral gastroenteritis

caseMeta.title: Medical-Surgical Telemetry: Adrenal (Addisonian) crisis in known Addison disease after viral gastroenteritis (24 hours, seven 4-hour checkpoints)
learningObjectives: Recognize adrenal crisis in a person with known adrenal insufficiency: hypotension and shock, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, hyperpigmentation, and the trigger (illness without extra steroid).
Give stress-dose IV hydrocortisone on time and explain why it also covers the missing aldosterone, why fludrocortisone is held at high doses and when it restarts.

Monitor and evaluate the response to treatment: blood pressure and orthostatic vitals, heart rate and rhythm, glucose, mental status, urine output, sodium (safe correction no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours) and potassium.
Teach adrenal insufficiency self-management with teach-back: sick-day rules, the emergency 100 mg IM hydrocortisone injection, medical alert ID and when to call 911.

problems.name: Adrenal crisis in primary adrenal insufficiency (autoimmune Addison disease, diagnosed 2021)
problems.details: Triggered by 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea with no steroid absorbed since Saturday morning; no emergency injection at home. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at 0420 (ED), then 50 mg IV every 6 hours.

problems.name: Hypovolemic shock (BP 74/40 at home), responding to fluid and hydrocortisone
problems.details: EMS saline 500 mL + 2 L saline + D5NS 150 mL/h. BP 98/60 lying, HR 104 at 0700. Orthostatic vitals when safe.

problems.name: Hypoglycemia (glucose 52 in the ED, 49 serum)
problems.details: Cortisol deficiency: no glucose production between meals. Dextrose 50% 0408; D5NS; POC glucose every 2 hours.

problems.name: Hyponatremia 126 mmol/L (hypovolemic, 2-3 days)
problems.details: Salt loss from aldosterone deficiency, vomiting and diarrhea, plus ADH release. Correction LIMIT 8 mmol/L in 24 hours.

problems.name: Hyperkalemia 6.0 mmol/L with peaked T waves
problems.details: Aldosterone deficiency and acute kidney injury. Normal PR and QRS. Telemetry; expected to fall with fluid and hydrocortisone.

problems.name: Acute gastroenteritis (son had the same illness)
problems.details: Vomiting and 6-8 watery stools a day since Saturday. Contact (enteric) precautions; stool C. difficile PCR and GI panel.

problems.name: Hashimoto hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 88 mcg
problems.details: TSH 4.6 (mildly high, common in untreated adrenal insufficiency). Dose unchanged; held Monday only.

problems.name: Sodium correcting too fast (126 to 132 in 9 hours) with a water diuresis
problems.details: Fluid changed to D5 0.45% NaCl 100 mL/h at 1530. Limit: 134 until 0400 Tuesday.

Continuous telemetry (cardiac monitoring)
orders.instructions: Indication: potassium 6.0 with peaked T waves (ED). Call for heart rate over 130 or under 50, new arrhythmia or a change in the T waves. Review the need when potassium is normal twice and the ECG is normal.

orders.name: Vital signs every hour x4, then every 2 hours until systolic BP is 100 or more twice, then every 4 hours; mental status every 4 hours

orders.instructions: Lying 5 minutes, then sitting/standing 1 and 3 minutes, with a second person. Stop if dizzy. Positive: systolic drop of 20 or more, diastolic drop of 10 or more, or heart rate rise of 30 or more (or symptoms).

SODIUM CORRECTION LIMIT: sodium may rise no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours (126 at 0406 Mon): keep it at 134 or lower until 0400 Tue. Call for sodium over 134 before 0400, urine over 250 mL/h for 2 hours in a row, or new confusion, headache, trouble speaking or swallowing

orders.name: Adrenal insufficiency self-management teaching with teach-back (patient AND husband): sick-day rules, emergency hydrocortisone 100 mg IM injection (demonstrate and return-demonstrate), medical alert ID, steroid emergency card, when to call 911 / go to the ED
orders.instructions: Sick-day rule 1: fever 100.4 F or more, or illness needing bed rest or antibiotics: double the daily dose; fever 102.2 F or more: triple it, until 24-48 hours after recovery. Rule 2: vomiting or diarrhea and cannot keep pills down (or vomits within 30 minutes of a dose, twice): inject 100 mg IM in the outer thigh and go to the ED / call 911. Surgery, dental procedures and childbirth need extra steroid: show the card.

stickyNotes.title: Adrenal crisis: what to watch
stickyNotes.body: Not enough cortisol (and aldosterone): low BP, fast heart rate, low glucose, low sodium, high potassium, vomiting, belly pain, confusion. Signs the hydrocortisone is working: BP up, heart rate down, glucose stable, alert, nausea gone, urine flowing, sodium up slowly, potassium down.

stickyNotes.title: Hydrocortisone ON TIME
stickyNotes.body: 50 mg IV every 6 hours: 1000, 1600, 2200, 0400. Never hold it for a "good" BP, a high glucose or a normal sodium. A vomited or late dose can bring the crisis back. Lost IV: it can be given IM; call the provider.

stickyNotes.title: Fludrocortisone is HELD (for now)

notes.title: ED Provider Note - Adrenal Crisis
notes.author: A. Brennan, MD
notes.summary: 46-year-old woman with known Addison disease in adrenal crisis after gastroenteritis: shock, glucose 52, Na 126, K 6.0, peaked T waves. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV 0420 after cortisol/ACTH draw; 2.5 L fluid; admit telemetry.
notes.body:
**Chief complaint**
Confusion, weakness, vomiting and diarrhea.

**History of present illness**
46-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency (autoimmune Addison disease, diagnosed 2021, 21-hydroxylase antibodies positive) on hydrocortisone 15 mg at 0700 and 5 mg at 1400 and fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily, and Hashimoto hypothyroidism on levothyroxine. Her son had gastroenteritis last week. Since Saturday afternoon she has had 6-8 watery stools a day and repeated vomiting. She vomited her hydrocortisone Saturday afternoon and Sunday morning and did not take extra doses or an injection (she has no kit and says nobody taught her sick-day rules). Sunday: dizzy on standing, salt craving, fell to her knees. Found confused on the bathroom floor at 0318.

**Exam**
T 99.8 F, HR 124, BP 78/44, RR 22, SpO2 97% RA. Lethargic, GCS 13, oriented to self. Diffuse hyperpigmentation with dark buccal and gum patches, darker palmar creases. Dry mucous membranes, flat neck veins, weak pulses, cool hands. Abdomen soft, diffusely tender, no guarding or rebound, hyperactive bowel sounds. No meningismus. No rash.

**Results**
Na 126, K 6.0, Cl 94, CO2 18 (anion gap 14), BUN 38, creatinine 1.6 (baseline 0.8), glucose 49, Ca 10.6, albumin 4.6, lactate 3.1, serum osmolality 264. Urine Na 48, urine osm 420, SG 1.026, ketones 2+. WBC 10.8 with eosinophils 7% (absolute 0.76). Hgb 14.6. Lipase, LFTs and troponin normal. Urine hCG negative. ECG: sinus tachycardia 118, peaked T waves V2-V4, normal PR and QRS. Chest x-ray clear.

**Medical decision making**
Adrenal crisis in known primary adrenal insufficiency, triggered by viral gastroenteritis with loss of oral steroid. The pattern fits both cortisol deficiency (shock, hypoglycemia, low sodium, eosinophilia) and aldosterone deficiency (high potassium, urine sodium high despite dehydration, prerenal kidney injury). Random cortisol and ACTH drawn at 0406, before treatment; treatment NOT delayed for results. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV given at 0420. Sepsis considered: no source besides the gut, lungs clear, UA clean; blood cultures sent, antibiotics not started (afebrile, improving with steroid and fluid; re-evaluate if fever or worsening). Potassium 6.0 with peaked T waves only (P waves present, normal PR and QRS, no arrhythmia): treat the cause (hydrocortisone and saline); insulin-dextrose NOT used because she is hypoglycemic; calcium gluconate considered and kept at the bedside, not given (QRS normal, potassium expected to fall quickly, calcium already 10.6). Continuous monitoring; give calcium for QRS widening or an arrhythmia. Recheck BMP in 4 hours. Sodium 126 is chronic (2-3 days): avoid raising it more than 8 in 24 hours.

**ED course**
D50 25 g (0408), hydrocortisone 100 mg IV (0420), NS 1 L x2, ondansetron 4 mg IV, D5NS 150 mL/h from 0600. BP 78/44 to 96/58, HR 124 to 104, glucose 52 to 96, more alert.

**Diagnoses**
1. Adrenal crisis, primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease).
2. Hypovolemic shock, resolving.
3. Hypoglycemia. 4. Hyponatremia (126). 5. Hyperkalemia (6.0) with peaked T waves.
6. Acute kidney injury, prerenal (creatinine 1.6).
7. Acute gastroenteritis, probably viral.

**Disposition**
Admit to the hospitalist (Dr. Osei), Med-Surg Telemetry 4 West. Endocrinology consult in the morning.

notes.title: Hospitalist Admission H&P
notes.author: K. Osei, MD
notes.summary: Admit telemetry: adrenal crisis (Addison disease) from viral gastroenteritis. Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h from 1000, D5NS 150 mL/h, BMP q4h, glucose q2h, fludrocortisone held, endocrine consult.
notes.body:
**Identification**
Lauren Mitchell, 46-year-old woman, middle school science teacher, lives with her husband Daniel (health care proxy) and son Ethan (15). Admitted 0640 Monday 12/07/2026.

**Chief complaint**
"I couldn't keep anything down, not even my pills."

**HPI**
See the ED note. Known autoimmune Addison disease (2021) with 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea (son had the same illness), no hydrocortisone absorbed since Saturday morning, no extra doses, no emergency injection. Arrived in shock with hypoglycemia, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Improving after hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at 0420 and 2.5 L of fluid.

**Past history**
Addison disease 2021 (presented with fatigue, weight loss, salt craving and tanning; 21-hydroxylase antibodies positive). Hashimoto hypothyroidism 2016. Appendectomy at age 19. No previous adrenal crisis. Last endocrinology visit 18 months ago (Dr. S. Kaur); was due for follow-up. Never prescribed an emergency hydrocortisone injection.

**Home medications**
Hydrocortisone 15 mg at 0700 and 5 mg at 1400. Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. Levothyroxine 88 mcg daily at 0600. Vitamin D3 2,000 units daily.

**Allergy**
Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim: hives.

**Social**
Never smoker, rare alcohol, no drugs. Very active; runs on weekends.

**Family history**
Mother with type 1 diabetes and vitiligo; sister with Hashimoto thyroiditis.

**Exam (0630)**
T 99.4 F, HR 104, BP 96/58, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA. Weight 58.2 kg (usual 61), height 165 cm. Drowsy, oriented to person and place, follows commands, no focal deficit. Hyperpigmented skin, palmar creases and buccal mucosa. Dry mucous membranes. Lungs clear. Heart regular, tachycardic, no murmur. Abdomen soft, mild diffuse tenderness, hyperactive bowel sounds. No edema. Bruises on both knees.

**Assessment**
Adrenal crisis in primary adrenal insufficiency, triggered by acute viral gastroenteritis and loss of oral replacement. Complications: hypovolemic shock (responding), hypoglycemia, hyponatremia 126 (hypovolemic, chronic), hyperkalemia 6.0 with peaked T waves (aldosterone deficiency), prerenal AKI, mild hypercalcemia (volume contraction). Eosinophilia fits cortisol deficiency.

**Plan**
1. Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours (1000, 1600, 2200, 0400) = 200 mg a day. Do not hold. Taper when eating and stable (endocrinology).
2. Fludrocortisone HELD: not needed while hydrocortisone is more than 50 mg a day. Home oral hydrocortisone held.
3. Fluids: D5NS 150 mL/h. Reassess lungs every 4 hours.
4. Sodium: BMP every 4 hours. Goal rise 4-6 per 24 hours, LIMIT 8 per 24 hours (no higher than 134 by 0400 Tuesday). Expect a brisk urine flow once cortisol and volume are back.
5. Potassium: telemetry; expected to fall with fluid and steroid. No binders. Repeat ECG 1330.
6. Glucose: POC every 2 hours x3, then every 4 hours. Hypoglycemia protocol (D50 if not safe to swallow).
7. GI: ondansetron PRN, NPO except sips, advance when nausea settles. Stool C. diff PCR and GI panel. Contact (enteric) precautions.
8. Possible infection: blood cultures pending; no antibiotics now.
9. Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine held today (vomiting); resume tomorrow. TSH 4.6 (mildly high, common in untreated adrenal insufficiency) with free T4 1.1 (0615): no dose change now.
10. VTE: enoxaparin 40 mg daily. Falls: high risk.
11. Consults: endocrinology, pharmacy (education, emergency kit), dietitian.
12. Code: Full. Proxy: husband.

notes.title: Pharmacy Medication History and Steroid Review
notes.author: T. Nakagawa, PharmD
notes.summary: Medication history verified. No emergency hydrocortisone kit ever dispensed; no sick-day rules teaching on record. Fludrocortisone hold is appropriate at 200 mg/day hydrocortisone. Hydrocortisone doses must be on time.
notes.body:
**Sources**
Patient (more alert now), husband, bottles from home, outpatient pharmacy fill history.

**Home medications (verified)**
- Hydrocortisone 10 mg tablets: 1.5 tablets (15 mg) on waking, 1/2 tablet (5 mg) at 1400. Fills on time. Last dose absorbed: Saturday 0700.
- Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily.
- Levothyroxine 88 mcg daily at 0600.
- Vitamin D3 2,000 units daily.
- No over-the-counter products, herbal supplements or other steroids. No opioids.

**Findings**
1. No hydrocortisone injection kit (Act-O-Vial) has ever been dispensed. No record of sick-day rules teaching. The patient says, "I thought if I threw it up I should just wait for the next dose."
2. She does not wear a medical alert ID.
3. Last endocrinology prescription renewal 18 months ago; refills from the primary care office since.

**Assessment / recommendations (discussed with Dr. Delacroix)**
- Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours is appropriate stress dosing. Mark as time critical: give within 30 minutes of the scheduled time.
- Fludrocortisone hold is appropriate: hydrocortisone at more than 50 mg/day has enough mineralocorticoid (aldosterone-like) effect. Restart when the dose is 50 mg/day or less.
- Levothyroxine: safe to miss one day; resume Tuesday 0600.
- Ondansetron: QTc 428, safe.
- Avoid drugs that speed up cortisol breakdown if possible later (for example rifampin, phenytoin) and remember that a patient on replacement needs extra steroid for surgery and procedures.
- Before discharge: two emergency kits (hydrocortisone 100 mg/2 mL Act-O-Vial) with syringes and needles, teaching with return demonstration for patient and husband, written sick-day rules, steroid emergency card, medical alert ID. Pharmacy will check insurance coverage for the kits.

**Event**

Hypoglycemia from cortisol deficiency (no glycogen stores, no glucose production by the liver) and nothing by mouth. The 0900 serum glucose was 74 (low normal) while on D5NS 150 mL/h. Asked the RN to confirm on the MAR that the hydrocortisone 50 mg due at 1000 was given on time (a late or missed dose is a common cause of relapse); even when on time, its effect on glucose takes several hours. 0900 BMP: Na 128, K 5.5, creatinine 1.4.

- Continue D5NS 150 mL/h (dextrose source).
- POC glucose every hour x2, then every 2 hours until three values are over 70, then every 4 hours.
- Clear liquids when nausea allows (endocrinology to see this afternoon). Ondansetron 4 mg IV now available (last dose 0430).

notes.title: Endocrinology Consult Note
notes.author: M. Harrington, MD
notes.summary: Adrenal crisis in autoimmune Addison disease, precipitated by viral gastroenteritis (GI panel pending) without sick-day dosing. Cortisol 1.8 before treatment. Continue hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h for 24 h, then oral taper; fludrocortisone held until hydrocortisone is 50 mg/day; safe sodium correction; full education before discharge.
notes.body:
**Reason for consult**
Adrenal crisis in known Addison disease.

**History**
As documented. Diagnosis 2021: fatigue, weight loss, salt craving, tanning; ACTH high, cortisol low, 21-hydroxylase antibodies positive. Stable on hydrocortisone 20 mg/day and fludrocortisone 0.1 mg. No prior crisis. Never given an emergency injection kit and never taught sick-day rules (our clinic will review why). Precipitant: viral gastroenteritis with vomiting of oral doses since Saturday.

**Exam (1330)**
Alert, oriented x3, still tired. BP 104/64 lying, HR 96. Mucous membranes moist. Hyperpigmentation of palmar creases, knuckles, gums and buccal mucosa; old appendectomy scar darker than the surrounding skin. Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness. No edema.

**Data**
Random cortisol (0406, before hydrocortisone): **1.8 mcg/dL** (in severe illness the cortisol should be well above 18). ACTH pending (expected high). Na 126 to 128 to 132 (1300). K 6.0 to 5.5 to 4.9. Creatinine 1.6 to 1.2. Glucose 58 at 1100 treated. Eosinophils 7%. TSH 4.6, free T4 1.1.

**Assessment**
1. Adrenal crisis, primary adrenal insufficiency, precipitated by gastroenteritis and missed steroid. Responding well.
2. Hyponatremia, now correcting quickly: +6 in 9 hours. As cortisol returns, ADH (the water-holding hormone) switches off and she will lose free water in the urine. Risk of correcting too fast.
3. Hyperkalemia, resolving (aldosterone deficiency; hydrocortisone at this dose acts on the same receptor).
4. Mildly high TSH: common in untreated adrenal insufficiency and usually settles with steroid. Do NOT change the levothyroxine dose now; recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks.

**Recommendations**
1. Continue hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours until Tuesday 0400 (last IV dose), then oral 20 mg / 20 mg / 10 mg on Tuesday, double home dose (30 mg + 10 mg) until the diarrhea has stopped 24 hours, then home dose 15 mg + 5 mg.
2. Fludrocortisone: keep HELD while hydrocortisone is more than 50 mg a day. Restart 0.1 mg daily on Tuesday 0800, the morning the dose drops to 50 mg/day.
3. Sodium: limit the rise to 8 mmol/L in 24 hours (no higher than 134 before 0400 Tuesday). Suggest a lower-sodium fluid now and close monitoring of urine output; if the limit is reached, D5W and/or desmopressin (discuss with us).
4. Advance to clear liquids; fluids to thirst. No sodium restriction for Addison disease long term, but no extra salt or salty broth while the sodium is rising quickly (until the 24-hour limit window ends).
5. Added renin and aldosterone to the 0406 ED sample (send-out, for the record).
6. Education before discharge (pharmacy and nursing): sick-day rules, two emergency injection kits with return demonstration (patient and husband), medical alert ID, steroid emergency card, letter for the school nurse/employer, when to call 911.
7. Clinic follow-up with me in 1-2 weeks.

notes.title: Endocrinology Addendum - ACTH Result
notes.author: M. Harrington, MD
notes.summary: ACTH 1,240 pg/mL (drawn before steroid) with cortisol 1.8: confirms PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency (the adrenal gland, not the pituitary). Explains the hyperpigmentation and the need for fludrocortisone.
notes.body:
**Result**
ACTH (0406, before hydrocortisone): **1,240 pg/mL** (normal 7.2-63).

**Interpretation**
Very low cortisol with very high ACTH = primary adrenal insufficiency (the adrenal glands do not respond, so the pituitary keeps sending more ACTH). ACTH comes from the same precursor (POMC) as melanocyte-stimulating hormone, which is why her skin, gums and scars darken. In primary disease aldosterone is also missing (salt wasting, high potassium), so she needs BOTH hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone for life. In secondary (pituitary) disease ACTH would be low, there would be no tanning and aldosterone would be normal.

No change to the plan.

Alert and oriented x3, no headache, speech normal. Glucose 118.

**Assessment**
1. Hyponatremia correcting too quickly. Cortisol and volume are back, so ADH has switched off and she is excreting dilute urine (water diuresis). At this pace she would pass the 8 mmol/L limit before 0400.
2. Still mildly volume depleted (orthostatic) despite good lying BP.
3. Adrenal crisis otherwise improving: alert, nausea gone, potassium 4.9, ECG normal (1330).

**Plan**
- Stop D5NS. Start D5 0.45% NaCl at 100 mL/h (less sodium, still volume and dextrose). Encourage oral fluids; clear liquids since 1345.
- Sodium limit 134 until 0400 Tuesday. BMP 1700 and 2100 as ordered. Call for sodium over 134, urine over 250 mL/h for 2 hours, or any neuro change; then D5W and/or desmopressin 1-2 mcg IV with endocrinology.
- Up with 1 assist only, dangle first. Repeat orthostatic vitals at 1900.
- Continue hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours (1600 due).

notes.title: Nutrition Initial Assessment
notes.author: E. Lindqvist, RD
notes.summary: Weight 58.2 kg (usual 61, -4.6% in 3 days from fluid loss). Tolerating clear liquids. Recommend regular diet, no sodium restriction, small frequent meals, fluids to thirst (no extra salty fluids while the sodium limit is on tonight); salt intake teaching for Addison disease.
notes.body:
**Assessment**
46-year-old woman with Addison disease admitted in adrenal crisis after 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea. Height 165 cm, weight 58.2 kg (usual 61 kg; loss mostly fluid). BMI 21.4. Clear liquids since 1400: broth, ginger ale, apple juice, about 480 mL, no vomiting. One loose stool 1640. Craving salt.

**Nutrition diagnosis**
Inadequate oral intake related to gastroenteritis and adrenal crisis, as shown by 2 days of vomiting and weight loss.

**Recommendations**
1. Advance to a regular diet, NO sodium restriction (discussed with Dr. Delacroix, who will place the order). Small, frequent meals; bland foods first (toast, rice, bananas, crackers, soup).
2. Oral rehydration: fluids to thirst, at least 2 L a day. Tonight, while the sodium limit is in place (Na 133 at 1700, limit 134 until 0400), offer water, juice and ginger ale rather than extra broth or salty fluids. After that, and on sick days at home, include salty fluids (broth, oral rehydration solution).
3. Teaching: people with Addison disease lose salt; they may salt food to taste and need extra salt and fluids in hot weather and with exercise or sweating. Do not follow a low-salt diet unless the endocrinologist says so.
4. Steroid with food to protect the stomach. Steroids raise appetite and glucose a little: a balanced diet.
5. Will follow up Tuesday.

notes.title: Night Hospitalist Progress Note
notes.author: K. Osei, MD
notes.summary: Stable: BP 116/72, HR 80, orthostatics negative at 1900, eating. Na 133 (1700, 2100), K 4.0. Norovirus on GI panel. Cannot sleep (steroid): melatonin PRN. Glucose 152 after dinner: steroid effect, no insulin.
notes.body:
**Interval**
RN called at 2310: patient cannot sleep, "wired", worried about her son and missing work. Glucose 152 at 2300 (dinner at 2000). No vomiting since 0440. One loose stool at 1640. Orthostatic vitals negative at 1900 (lying 112/70 HR 86; standing 104/66 HR 96). Walking with assist. Drinking well; regular dinner 75% eaten.

**Data**
1700: Na 133, K 4.4, creatinine 1.0, glucose 112. 2100: Na 133, K 4.0, creatinine 0.9, glucose 128. GI panel: norovirus detected; C. difficile negative.

**Assessment and plan**
1. Adrenal crisis resolving. Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV due 2200 and 0400. Endocrinology plans the oral switch Tuesday morning.
2. Sodium 133 and stable since 1700 after the fluid change: on track (limit 134 until 0400).
3. Potassium falling as expected (6.0 to 4.0). Mg/phos with the 0100 labs. Replace if 3.5 or lower (still falling, ongoing stool losses, fludrocortisone restarts Tuesday).
4. Insomnia from high-dose steroid and the setting: sleep hygiene, lights down, cluster care; melatonin 3 mg once PRN. No diphenhydramine or benzodiazepines (falls at night with a water diuresis and an IV).
5. Glucose 152: expected with stress-dose steroid in a person without diabetes. No insulin; call if over 180 twice.
6. Norovirus: contact (enteric) precautions and soap and water until 48 hours after the diarrhea stops. Husband and son: hand hygiene and clean bathrooms with a bleach product at home.

notes.title: Night Hospitalist Event Note - Lightheaded in the Bathroom; IV Site
notes.author: K. Osei, MD
notes.summary: Called 0250: walked to the bathroom alone at 0240, lightheaded, sat down on the toilet and called; no fall, no injury. Vitals and glucose stable per RN. Right forearm IV puffy and cool (infiltration): remove it and move the fluid to the left forearm IV. K 3.7.
notes.body:
**Event**
RN called at 0250. At about 0240 the patient got up without calling (bed alarm sounded), walked to the bathroom, felt lightheaded after a soft loose stool, sat on the toilet and pulled the call cord. No fall, no head strike. RN reports vitals stable and glucose 128 at 0300. She says she "didn't want to bother anyone."
RN also reports the 20 g right forearm IV site is puffy, pale and cool, about 3 cm of swelling (infiltration of D5 0.45% NaCl).

**Data**
0100: Na 133, K 3.7, creatinine 0.9, glucose 136, Mg 1.9, phos 2.9.

**Assessment and plan**
1. Near-fall at night: diuresis, steroid, hospital bed, lightheaded after straining. Not an adrenal relapse (BP normal, alert, glucose normal). Reinforce call-don't-fall, bed alarm, bedside commode tonight, non-skid socks, light on in the bathroom.
2. Infiltration: stop the infusion and remove the right forearm IV; run D5 0.45% NaCl through the 18 g left forearm IV; elevate the arm, compress per policy (non-vesicant fluid), mark and measure, reassess every hour. Keep one working IV (in case an IV steroid dose is needed); a second IV only if needed.
3. Potassium 3.7, falling by about 0.3-0.4 every 4 hours. Recheck at 0500; replace if 3.5 or lower.
4. Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV due 0400 through the left forearm IV.

notes.title: Night Hospitalist Note - Morning Labs
notes.author: K. Osei, MD
notes.summary: 0500: Na 134 (+8 in 25 h, at the limit, not over), K 3.5: KCl 20 mEq PO now; BMP 1300. Hgb 14.6 to 11.9 with rehydration. Eosinophils gone (0.4%). Blood cultures no growth at 24 h.
notes.body:
**Data (0500)**
Na 134, K 3.5, Cl 103, CO2 23, BUN 13, creatinine 0.8 (back to baseline), glucose 118, Ca 8.9, Mg 1.8, phos 3.1, albumin 3.6. CBC: WBC 12.6 (steroid effect), Hgb 11.9 (14.6 on arrival, diluted by rehydration), platelets 231, eosinophils 0.4% (7% on arrival). Blood cultures: no growth at 24 hours. Weight 59.8 kg.

**Assessment and plan**
1. Sodium 126 to 134 in 25 hours (+8): at the limit but not over it. No further correction needed; she will drink to thirst. Recheck with the 1300 BMP.
2. Potassium 3.5 (6.0 on arrival). Potassium chloride 20 mEq by mouth now with a snack; BMP at 1300. Fludrocortisone restarting at 0800 will also lower potassium: watch.
3. Hemoglobin fall is dilutional (no bleeding). Recheck at the endocrine follow-up.
4. White count 12.6 with no fever: expected after high-dose steroid (white cells leave the vessel walls). Not an infection.
5. Hand off to Dr. Delacroix at 0700. Endocrinology has written the oral transition orders.

notes.title: Endocrinology Progress Note - Transition to Oral Replacement
notes.author: M. Harrington, MD
notes.summary: Crisis resolved. Last IV hydrocortisone 0400. Oral hydrocortisone 20/20/10 mg today from 1000, double home dose until diarrhea stops 24 h, then 15 mg + 5 mg. Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg restarts 0800. Discharge this afternoon after teaching and return demonstration of the IM kit.
notes.body:
**Subjective**
"I feel almost normal. I want to go home to my son." Ate 75% of her dinner and toast overnight. One soft stool at 0240. No vomiting since 0440 yesterday. Some trouble sleeping.

**Objective**
Overnight vitals stable: BP 116-118/72-74, HR 76-80, afebrile. Orthostatic vitals negative at 1900 and 2300 per nursing. Alert and oriented x4. Na 134, K 3.5, creatinine 0.8, glucose 118.

**Evaluation of the treatment (criteria met)**
- Blood pressure normal without vasopressors; orthostatics negative.
- Heart rate under 100; telemetry normal sinus; peaked T waves gone (ECG 1330).
- Mental status back to baseline.
- Glucose stable 104-152 since 1300 without dextrose boluses.
- Sodium up safely (126 to 134 in 25 hours); potassium normal (low normal).
- Creatinine back to baseline (0.8); urine output good.
- Nausea gone, eating and drinking; diarrhea slowing.

**Plan**
1. Oral hydrocortisone today: 20 mg at 1000, 20 mg at 1500, 10 mg at 2000 (50 mg/day). Wednesday and Thursday: 30 mg on waking + 10 mg at 1400 (double the home dose) until the diarrhea has stopped for 24 hours. Then home dose 15 mg on waking + 5 mg at 1400.
2. Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily: RESTART at 0800 today (hydrocortisone now 50 mg/day). Check BP, swelling and potassium at follow-up.
3. Potassium chloride 20 mEq once (Dr. Osei). BMP 1300.
4. Levothyroxine resumed 0600; TSH in 6-8 weeks.
5. Teaching with teach-back (patient and husband) before discharge: sick-day rules, IM injection return demonstration, medical alert ID, steroid emergency card, school/employer letter.
6. Two emergency kits prescribed. Clinic follow-up with me in 1-2 weeks (case management to schedule).
7. Discharge this afternoon if she keeps the 1000 and 1500 doses down, eats lunch, orthostatics stay negative and the 1300 potassium is normal.

notes.title: Pharmacy Discharge Teaching Plan - Steroid Safety
notes.author: T. Nakagawa, PharmD
notes.summary: Teaching plan for patient and husband: daily doses, sick-day rules, emergency 100 mg IM hydrocortisone kit (Act-O-Vial) with return demonstration, card and ID. Kit covered by insurance ($15 copay each).
notes.body:
**Medication changes**
- Hydrocortisone taper (endocrinology): today 20/20/10 mg; Wed-Thu 30 mg + 10 mg; then home 15 mg + 5 mg. Take with food. Use a pill organizer and phone alarms.
- Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily restarts today.
- Levothyroxine 88 mcg on an empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before breakfast (unchanged).

**Sick-day rules (written handout, teach-back)**
1. Fever of 100.4 F or more, or an illness that needs bed rest or antibiotics: DOUBLE the daily hydrocortisone dose. Fever of 102.2 F or more: TRIPLE it. Continue until 24-48 hours after feeling well, then return to the usual dose. Call the endocrinology clinic.
2. Vomiting or diarrhea: if a dose is vomited within 30 minutes, take it again. If vomiting happens again, or there is severe diarrhea, or she cannot keep pills down: GIVE THE EMERGENCY INJECTION and call 911 or go to the ED.
3. Never stop or skip hydrocortisone. Always carry extra tablets.
4. Tell every provider and dentist she takes steroid replacement: surgery, procedures, childbirth and serious injuries need extra steroid. Show the steroid emergency card.

**Emergency hydrocortisone kit (hydrocortisone sodium succinate 100 mg/2 mL Act-O-Vial)**
1. Press the plunger cap to push the liquid into the powder; swirl gently (do not shake) until clear.
2. Clean the top, draw up all 2 mL with a 3 mL syringe, change to a 1-1.5 inch needle.
3. Inject into the middle of the outer thigh (vastus lateralis) at 90 degrees; through clothing is acceptable in an emergency.
4. Then call 911 or go to the ED and show the card: she still needs IV fluids and care.
Return demonstration with a training vial by the patient AND the husband (the person who gives it may be the husband if she is confused). Keep one kit at home and one in her bag; check the expiration date every 6 months; store at room temperature.

**Other**
- Medical alert ID (bracelet or necklace) "Adrenal insufficiency - steroid dependent".
- Insurance: kits covered, $15 copay each. Prescriptions sent to her pharmacy.
